To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the problems of containment, equivalence, minimality, and nonminality of conjunctive queries under key-based dependencies are in NP and that the same problems for queries over finite databases are in NP for the case of width one inclusion dependencies.

(1) the problems of query equivalence, containment, and nonmininality remain in NP for inclusion dependencies, (2) the problems are substantially more difficult for functional dependencies, and (3) the problems are not harder for inclusion dependencies than they are for functional dependencies if the set of dependencies satisfies a certain “key-based” condition.

the containment problem for conjunctive queries remains in NP when the only dependencies are inclusion dependencies, and that it remains in NP for conjunctive and union queries when all dependencies are key-based.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the containment of a query Q1 by another query Q2, when both queries are conjunctive queries and the underlying relational database is constrained by functional or inclusion dependencies.
the containment and equivalence problems for conjunctive queries under functional dependencies, inclusion dependencies, or both.

the following problems: (1) Given a set of dependencies and a query, determine whether the query can be rewritten to a smaller one that is equivalent on the database instance defined by the dependencies, (2) Given a query, determine the set of all possible equivalent queries, and (3) Given a set S of queries, find the minimal subset T of S such that every query in S is equivalent to one in T.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of inclusion dependency does not make the optimization of relational database queries any harder when the set of dependencies has one of the two forms mentioned above.
the containment and equivalence problems are in NP for finite or infinite databases when either (a), (b), or (c) holds, where (c) is “the set of dependencies is key-based and has width one.”

, in the presence of inclusion and functional dependencies, containment, equivalence, minimality, and non-minimality are NP-hard, but that there are substantial subclasses for which the problems are in NP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the problems of containment and equivalence remain tractable in the presence of functional and inclusion dependencies, but the problems of nonminimality and minimization are in general intractable.
the containment problem is in NP when the dependencies are inclusion dependencies, or key-based, or both.
inclusion dependencies do not make optimization any harder than when there are only functional dependencies, except in the case of infinite databases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in many cases of interest, inclusion dependencies do not add much complexity to the basic optimization problems.
the presence of inclusion dependency does not make optimization of conjunctive queries any more difficult than it is in the presence of functional dependencies alone, and may make it easier.
inclusion dependencies do not complicate the optimization problem as much as they might seem to at first sight.
